isoNews2006.title: Why did ISBN users begin making New Year 2007 resolutions in 2005?
isoNews2006.author: International Organization for Standardization
isoNews2006.quote: The fourth edition of ISO 2108, Information and documentation – International Standard Book Number (ISBN),published in 2005, became necessary because the very success of the ISBN system, up to now based on 10 digits, has been causing it to run out of capacity.

'ISO 2108:2005, Information and documentation – International Standard Book Number (ISBN), costs 99 Swiss francs'

bowkerHistory.title: ISBN History (US ISBN Agency)
bowkerHistory.author: R. R. Bowker LLC, isbn.org
bowkerHistory.quote: In 1965, W. H. Smith (the largest single book retailer in Great Britain) announced its plans to move to a computerized warehouse in 1967 and wanted a standard numbering system for books it carried.
supports: 'They hired consultants to work on behalf of their interest, the British Publishers Association's Distribution and Methods Committee and other experts in the U.K. book trade.'
'They devised the Standard Book Numbering (SBN) system in 1966 and it was implemented in 1967.'
The page is undated; year recorded as the year the page was read. It names no individual designer.
'the International Standard Book Number (ISBN) was approved as an ISO standard in 1970, and became ISO 2108'

isoFocus2011.title: From Dickens to Dante: ISBN propels book trade to billions, ISO Focus+, April 2011, Special Report
isoFocus2011.author: Stella Griffiths, International ISBN Agency
isoFocus2011.quote: In the United Kingdom (UK) , a prototype (nine-digit) numbering system that included a final validation character quickly gained acceptance from 1967.
supports: 'In response to the perceived pressure on available numbers, the ISBN standard underwent a fourth revision in 2005, changing the length of the identifier to 13 digits and thereby almost doubling its capacity.'
'Local agencies assign ISBN prefixes with the appropriate range of individual ISBNs for each publisher's anticipated output'
'More than 160 ISBN agencies serving more than 200 countries and territories have collectively assigned more than one million ISBN prefixes to publishers.'
'ISBN (based on the original UK system, but now a 10-digit identifier) was approved as an International Standard in 1970.'
'A principal benefit of the 13-digit solution enables the ISBN system to make use of a new “979” EAN prefix which was reserved years ago for the future use of the book trade within the EAN system.'

unverified: That Gordon Foster wrote a 1966 report for W. H. Smith. Neither official agency history names an individual: R. R. Bowker's isbn.org says W. H. Smith 'hired consultants' who, with the Publishers Association's Distribution and Methods Committee, 'devised the Standard Book Numbering (SBN) system in 1966 and it was implemented in 1967'; the International ISBN Agency's Users' Manual credits the firms 'J. Whitaker & Sons, Ltd.' (UK, 1967) and 'R. R. Bowker' (US, 1968). The Wikipedia claim carries a 'citation needed' tag. The one biographical source found, Trinity College Dublin's School of Computer Science and Statistics history page for Frederic Gordon Foster (https://www.tcd.ie/scss/about/history/gordon-foster/), says Foster was commissioned in 1966 by the publisher Wiley — not by W. H. Smith — and was then 'consulted by the Publishers Association'; it also telescopes the chronology, attributing the ten-digit international scheme to the same 1967 report, which conflicts with ISO Focus+ and the Users' Manual (ISO approval 1970). It is a centenary memorial essay, not a document of record, and is deliberately not cited. What is confirmed is the Library of Congress record for F. G. Foster, 'Standard numbering in the book trade', Publishers Association, London, 1967, 9 p. The prose claims only that.

That W. H. Smith's warehouse problem is what produced Foster's report. REMOVED IN FACT-CHECK: the prose previously read 'The answer was nine pages: F. G. Foster...', which joins the two causally. No opened source supports the join, and two cut against it — Bowker dates the SBN scheme to 1966, a year before the report, and Trinity College Dublin names Wiley as Foster's commissioning client. The two facts are now stated side by side with no connective, and card p3c01-c1's prompt no longer calls the report 'the report that settled the scheme'.

That Foster's report is the document that fixed the nine-digit width. The Library of Congress record attests the report's author, publisher, date and nine-page length; ISO Focus+ separately attests that a nine-digit scheme with a final validation character 'quickly gained acceptance from 1967'. Nothing opened joins them. Card p3c01-c1 no longer asks 'how wide was the number?' and no longer answers 'nine digits' from a card whose only source is the catalogue record.

The subtitle 'an inquiry carried out by the Publishers Association'. REMOVED IN FACT-CHECK from card p3c01-c1: the claim is true — OpenLibrary edition OL21503720M carries it, from a Talis MARC contribution — but the card's only source is the Library of Congress MARCXML record, whose 245$b reads simply 'a report'. Rather than add a second ledger entry for one clause, the card now makes the same point from a field the cited record does carry, MARC 650: 'Publishers' standard book numbers -- Standards -- Great Britain'.

That a publisher, once given a registrant element, numbers its own books 'forever'. REMOVED IN FACT-CHECK from the prose and from card p3c01-c4: contradicted by the cited source itself, ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed. §5.3 — 'Once they have exhausted the allocation of ISBNs that is linked to their registrant element, they may be assigned an additional registrant element' — and by §14.4. Coordination is paid once per block, not once per publisher, which is also the chapter's own design (lease a million, come back for the next million).

That it was nine digits that ran out. CORRECTED IN FACT-CHECK: the closing line read 'because nine digits had once looked like plenty', but the ISO news item quoted three sentences earlier says the system was 'up to now based on 10 digits'. The nine-digit UK scheme was widened to ten before ISO adopted it (ISO Focus+ 2011: 'based on the original UK system, but now a 10-digit identifier'). The prose now carries that widening and closes on ten.

That barcodes changed on 1 January 2007. REMOVED IN FACT-CHECK: the closing line read 'Every catalogue, till and barcode plate on earth changed primary key that day'. Books had carried Bookland EAN-13 barcodes for decades, and ISO Focus+ 2011 describes the thirteen-digit move as making 'use of a new “979” EAN prefix' and dovetailing with the EAN.UCC system — i.e. the ISBN was widened to match the barcode, not the other way round. The line now reads 'Every catalogue and till on earth'.

That the ten-digit space ran out because individual publishers' forecasts were wrong. REMOVED IN FACT-CHECK: the prose opened its third paragraph with 'The forecasts were wrong.' The ISO news item attributes the pressure to 'the very success of the ISBN system' and to 'the explosive growth of electronic publishing', and names no registration group and no mis-sized block. The paragraph now opens 'Then the space ran out', which is what the source says.

The text of Foster's report. Only the Library of Congress catalogue record and the OpenLibrary edition record were opened, not the nine pages themselves; no quotation from the report appears anywhere.

The personal roles of David Whitaker and Emery Koltay. The Users' Manual names the firms — J. Whitaker & Sons, Ltd. (UK, 1967) and R. R. Bowker (US, 1968) — not the individuals. Neither name appears in the prose or on a card.
That the English-language registration groups specifically were exhausted by 2005. The ISO news item names no registration group. No group-level claim is made.

Any figure for what the ISBN-13 migration cost the book trade. The only currency figure found and used is the 99 Swiss franc list price of ISO 2108:2005, stated on the ISO news page. It is the price of the document, not the cost of the migration.
That ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 still coexist in library and retail databases today. Not claimed in the prose.

Date conflict, recorded and avoided: the International ISBN Agency's own ISQ article 'ISBN: A History' (Stella Griffiths, ISQ vol. 27 no. 2&3, 2015) dates ISO's first publication of ISBN to 1972, while the same agency's Users' Manual (7th ed.) and its ISO Focus+ article both say 1970 (ISO 2108:2017's own Introduction says 'Since its inception in 1970'). No bare ISO-approval year appears in the prose.
